arXiv:2610.38090v1 [cs.IR] 28 Oct 2026

Predicting What Answer Engines Cite:
Open Decision Models, Rerankers and a Distilled 4B Student
on Ten Engines under Controlled RetrievalThanks: The model, the benchmark, the predictions and the code are released; see Section 8.

Elisha Bajemon Affiliation: TW3 Partners (Citead) Email: e.bajemon@tw3partners.com    André-Louis Rochet Affiliation: TW3 Partners (Citead) Email: arochet@tw3partners.com
October 2026
Abstract

Generative engine optimization needs a scorer that ranks candidate pages by the share of an answer they will receive as citations. We measure pretrained rerankers, a hosted typed decision model (Jev), eight open decision models and distilled students on GEO-Bench queries answered by ten engines that receive the same candidate sources in their prompt. Where several engines answer the same query, they agree with one another at a within-group Spearman correlation of 0.704. Jev and two open 27B decision models, used without training, are the strongest scorers at 0.575 to 0.578. A Qwen3-Reranker-4B fine-tuned with low-rank adapters on teacher labels for other GEO-Bench queries, released as GEO Citation Ranker 4B, reaches 0.542 to 0.549 across three seeds, and its differences with the 27B models and with Jev are not distinguishable from zero on 229 queries. Most of the remaining distance between the student and Jev disappears when Jev scores one passage at a time, as the student does. Students trained on teacher labels and on observed engine citations reach the same level, and labels from Jev alone match the two-teacher target at 0.6B. We release the model, the benchmark, the predictions of every reported scorer and the code.

1 Introduction

Work on generative engine optimization (GEO) asks, for a given query, which of the candidate pages an answer engine will draw on, and how much (Aggarwal et al., 2024). Measuring engines directly answers it, but each measurement is paid, slow and non-deterministic, so practitioners increasingly use a model to predict the answer before any engine is queried. Pretrained rerankers are free to run and were trained for topical relevance (Nogueira et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). LLM judges prompted with a rubric can rank sources, at the cost of one generation per group (Zheng et al., 2023). Typed decision models, such as the hosted Jev (TypeSafe, 2026; Shea and Roche, 2026), return a probability distribution over a fixed scale for each question asked about a state. Several open decision models were published on the Hugging Face Hub after Jev’s release (autotrust, 2026; Perplexity AI, 2026; TokenRhythm, 2026; Mapika, 2026; manjunathshiva, 2026; jaredpalmer, 2026; convaiinnovations, 2026). We know of no measurement of decision models or distilled rerankers against the citations of answer engines.

This paper measures them on one benchmark of 229 GEO-Bench queries (GEO-Optim, 2024). Each query is answered by one to ten engines that receive the same five candidate sources in their prompt, and the label of a source is its citation share in the answer. For the 150 queries answered by several engines, the benchmark also measures how far the engines agree with each other, which gives every scorer a reference that comes from the engines themselves.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it reports the agreement between engines and the level of 36 scorer configurations on the same 1220 engine-query groups, with intervals clustered by query and paired differences (Section 6). Second, it shows that two open 27B decision models match the hosted judge without training, and that presenting the five candidates together accounts for most of the distance between Jev and a single-passage student. Third, it distils teacher labels into Qwen3-Reranker students at 0.6B, 4B and 8B, releases the 4B student as GEO Citation Ranker 4B, and separates the effect of teacher choice, label volume, capacity and observed citations.

2 Related work

Generative engine optimization.

Aggarwal et al. (2024) introduced GEO and GEO-Bench and reported citation gains from content edits. Later work measured conversational SEO on its own benchmark (Puerto et al., 2025), ranked the factors of competition between two sources (Vishwakarma et al., 2026), separated being cited from shaping the answer (Zhang et al., 2026), and repaired document-specific citation failures with agents (Tian et al., 2026). Adversarial manipulation of conversational search rankings was demonstrated by Pfrommer et al. (2024). Bajemon and Rochet (2026) re-measured the 2023 content levers on ten current engines and found that query-agnostic content scores predict citation only weakly. This paper uses the engine answers collected for that study.

Citation in generated answers.

Generated answers often cite sources that do not support them (Liu et al., 2023), and citation quality can be evaluated and trained for (Gao et al., 2023). LLMs also use the middle of a long context less than its ends (Liu et al., 2024), which predicts an effect of source position in our prompts.

LLM rerankers and distillation.

LLMs rerank well zero-shot (Sun et al., 2023), and their rankings can be distilled into smaller open models (Pradeep et al., 2023a; Pradeep et al., 2023b) or used to generate training data (Bonifacio et al., 2022), following the general recipe of knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015). Qwen3-Reranker frames relevance as a yes or no answer scored by token probabilities (Zhang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). We train with a pairwise logistic loss (Burges et al., 2005) and low-rank adapters (Hu et al., 2022).

Judges.

LLM-as-a-judge is standard for graded criteria (Zheng et al., 2023), and judges are sensitive to the order in which candidates are presented (Wang et al., 2023). Typed decision models were introduced for binary agent-evaluation criteria (Shea and Roche, 2026); we apply them to a graded, comparative criterion.

3 Problem statement

Problem 1 (Citation ranking).

An engine ee answers query qq from five candidate sources s1,…,s5s_{1},\dots,s_{5} given in its prompt in that order. A scorer sees qq and the source texts, never the engine’s answer, and must rank the five sources by the citation share each receives in the answer.

Definition 1 (Citation share).

The label ye,q,iy_{e,q,i} of source sis_{i} is its position-adjusted word count share: the words of each answer sentence citing sis_{i}, weighted by the sentence’s position in the answer, summed and normalised over the five sources (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Bajemon and Rochet, 2026).

Definition 2 (Score).

For a scorer with predictions y^\hat{y}, the score of a group (e,q)(e,q) is the Spearman correlation between y^⋅\hat{y}_{\cdot} and ye,q,⋅y_{e,q,\cdot} over the five sources, with average ranks for ties and zero for a constant prediction. The benchmark score is the mean over groups whose five labels are not all equal.

Definition 3 (Cross-engine agreement).

For a group (e,q)(e,q), the cross-engine agreement is the score of the predictor y^i=meane′≠e⁡ye′,q,i\hat{y}_{i}=\operatorname{mean}_{e^{\prime}\neq e}y_{e^{\prime},q,i}, the mean label that the other engines answering qq give to source sis_{i}. It is defined for queries answered by at least two engines.

Cross-engine agreement uses information that no scorer has, namely other engines’ answers to the same prompt. It measures how much of a group’s ranking is shared across engines. It serves as a reference for the scorers and is not an upper bound on them.

4 Benchmark and scorers

Evaluation data.

The 229 queries are the GEO-Bench test queries for which Bajemon and Rochet (2026) collected engine answers, with the prompt, decoding settings and citation parser described in that work (temperature 0, pinned model identifiers). Each source is represented by the first 320 words of its raw text. The ten engines are listed with their vendor and coverage in Appendix A. Seventy-nine queries are answered by one engine, 50 by five, 23 by seven to nine and 77 by all ten, which gives 1220 non-degenerate groups over 1145 passages. Every engine receives the query and the five sources in its prompt, and no engine retrieves documents. The benchmark therefore measures citation under controlled retrieval, the setting of GEO-Bench.

Pretrained rerankers.

We score the NIM reranker (rerank-qa-mistral-4b), bge-reranker-v2-m3 and Qwen3-Reranker at 0.6B, 4B and 8B with their default inference code and no training, on the same 320-word passages.

Typed decision models.

A typed decision model receives a state and a set of questions and returns, for each question, a probability distribution over the answer levels (Shea and Roche, 2026). We ask one six-level question per passage, from level 0 (not cited) to level 5 (the answer relies mainly on this passage), and the score is the expectation over levels. The wording is given in Appendix B. In the listwise protocol the state holds the query and the five passages and the five questions are asked in one call; in the pointwise protocol the state holds the query and one passage. Passages are truncated to 250 words in the state, which is shorter than the text engines and rerankers receive. We score the hosted Jev 1.13 (snapshot 20260917) through its API, and eight open models from the Hugging Face Hub with the runtime of their model cards. The eight were chosen before any was scored, as the most downloaded or best placed on their own model cards among those that accept an ordered score question. The same state and questions are used for every model, with no prompt tuning.

Distilled students.

The training data are 757 groups of five sources, one for each GEO-Bench test query outside the evaluation set that has five sources, prepared with the same 320-word recipe. None has engine labels. Two teachers label each group. Jev scores it in the listwise protocol, for 0.10 USD over the whole set. An LLM judge produces synthetic labels for batches of six groups, on a 0 to 100 scale, with the rubric of Appendix B. The two teachers agree at a mean per-group Spearman of 0.759. The default target is the mean of the two teachers, each rescaled to [0,1][0,1]; ablations use one teacher. Students are Qwen3-Reranker models at 0.6B, 4B and 8B scored by the log-odds of “yes” against “no” after an instruction asking whether an answer engine would cite the passage. A rank-16 adapter on all attention and feed-forward projections is trained with a pairwise logistic loss within each group, over the pairs whose targets differ by more than 0.05 and weighted by that difference, for four epochs at learning rate 10−410^{-4}. The 4B student trains in about two hours on one RTX 3090. The 4B student trained with seed 42 is released as GEO Citation Ranker 4B.

5 Evaluation protocol

Intervals are 95% percentile bootstraps over queries, so that the groups of one query are resampled together (Field and Welsh, 2007), with 1000 resamples and a fixed seed. Every comparison between two scorers is a paired difference on the groups both cover, and we call two scorers indistinguishable when the 95% interval of their difference covers zero. Equivalence within a margin of 0.05 is tested by two one-sided tests, which require the 90% interval of the difference to lie inside the margin (Lakens, 2017). As a second metric we report top-1 accuracy, the share of groups where the scorer’s top source is a most-cited source. Because the 77 queries answered by all ten engines contribute most groups, we also report the mean per engine and per query.

Students trained on observed citations are evaluated by five-fold cross-validation over the evaluation queries, with a fixed assignment of queries to folds, and each group is scored only by the model that did not see its query. Fifteen evaluation passages share their first 40 words with a training source, because GEO-Bench reuses pages. Removing the 57 groups that contain them changes the score of any student by at most 0.006 and lowers the 4B student by 0.003.

6 Results

Result 1 (engines agree more than scorers predict).

On the 1141 groups whose query has at least two engines, the engines agree with one another at 0.704 [0.669, 0.737] (Table 1, Figure 1). The agreement is 0.689 [0.652, 0.723] when engines of the same vendor are excluded from the mean. It exceeds Jev by 0.126 [0.083, 0.175] and the 4B student by 0.159 [0.116, 0.201] on the same groups. Engines give the first source a mean share of 0.234 and the fifth 0.164, and ranking by position alone scores 0.131, the same as BM25. Adding the source position to a scorer’s ranking, with a weight fitted on four folds and applied to the fifth, changes the student by +0.011 [−-0.002, +0.025] and Jev by −-0.013 [−-0.023, −-0.005]. The distance between the scorers and the engines’ agreement is therefore not explained by source position.

Result 2 (open 27B decision models match the hosted judge).

Used without training, JEV-27B and pplx-decider-27B reach 0.578 and 0.575, against 0.575 for the hosted Jev. Their paired differences with Jev are +0.003 [−-0.034, +0.036] and 0.000 [−-0.028, +0.031]. Scores fall as model size decreases: JEV-9B reaches 0.516, the four open 4B decision models 0.44 to 0.50 with their better protocol, and a 0.4B encoder 0.214. The pretrained rerankers range from 0.341 to 0.452, and the 8B reranker is not above the 4B (−-0.004 [−-0.043, +0.035]).

Result 3 (GEO Citation Ranker 4B is not distinguishable from the 27B models).

The 4B student scores 0.542 with seed 42, the released GEO Citation Ranker 4B, and 0.546 and 0.549 with two other seeds, and the largest difference between seeds is 0.007, with an interval covering zero. Fine-tuning adds 0.090 [0.059, 0.121] over the same reranker without training. Its differences with JEV-27B (−-0.037 [−-0.080, +0.013]), pplx-decider-27B (−-0.033 [−-0.070, +0.005]), Jev (−-0.033 [−-0.072, +0.006]) and JEV-9B (+0.026 [−-0.015, +0.072]) all cover zero. Equivalence with Jev at a margin of 0.05 is not established, since the 90% interval of Jev’s lead over the mean of the three seeds is [−-0.002, +0.060]. Taken one comparison at a time, the student is above each of the four open 4B decision models, by 0.048 to 0.104. On top-1 accuracy the student (0.567), Jev (0.563), JEV-27B (0.566) and pplx-decider-27B (0.580) are within 0.02 of one another, against 0.476 for the reranker without training. Weighting each engine or each query equally gives the same picture with lower levels: per query, the student scores 0.529, Jev 0.562 and JEV-27B 0.553 (Appendix A).

Result 4 (one passage at a time, the student matches Jev).

Asked one passage at a time, Jev falls from 0.575 to 0.529 (−-0.046 [−-0.087, −-0.009]) and JEV-27B from 0.578 to 0.540 (−-0.038 [−-0.071, −-0.004]). Under that protocol the student’s differences with Jev (+0.012 [−-0.026, +0.056]) and JEV-27B (+0.001 [−-0.036, +0.040]) are close to zero. It scores above JEV-9B (+0.074 [0.022, 0.128]). For pplx-decider-27B and the smaller decision models the protocol effect is not distinguishable from zero (Table 2). Scoring the five candidates together is the natural next step for the student.

Result 5 (Jev labels and a quarter of the queries suffice).

At 0.6B, labels from Jev alone give 0.467, labels from the LLM judge alone 0.444 and their mean 0.457, and no pairwise difference excludes zero (Table 3). A quarter of the training queries, 189, gives 0.537 at 4B against 0.542 with all 757 (+0.005 [−-0.017, +0.027]); at 0.6B the difference is 0.030 [−-0.001, +0.060]. Adding groups that mix sources from different queries changes nothing detectable. A 4B student trained on observed citations of the evaluation queries, by five-fold cross-validation over 183 or 184 queries per fold, reaches 0.541. At matched volume, the student trained on teacher labels for 189 queries is not distinguishable from it (−-0.004 [−-0.041, +0.028]). Fine-tuning the teacher-trained student on observed citations gives 0.562, a gain of 0.020 [−-0.010, +0.051].

Result 6 (capacity stops paying at 4B).

With identical labels and recipe, the 4B student is above the 0.6B by 0.085 [0.051, 0.119]. The 8B student is not above the 4B (−-0.009 [−-0.032, +0.015] at seed 42), and its two seeds differ by 0.026 [0.008, 0.046], whereas the three 4B seeds do not differ.

7 Threats to validity

Controlled retrieval.

Engines receive five fixed sources in their prompt, so the benchmark measures which provided source an engine cites, and not whether a search engine retrieves a page. This removes retrieval noise from the label. It does not establish that the ranking transfers to engines that search the web, which would require answers collected from live search products.

Teachers and inputs.

The student targets combine Jev and one LLM judge with one rubric. At 0.6B, Jev labels alone train a student as good as the two-teacher target. Jev is a hosted model versioned by its provider, and the open 27B decision models offer a teacher with frozen weights. Decision models see 250 words of each passage, against 320 for engines and students, which can only work against them.

Scope of the measurements.

The benchmark is English, built from one source dataset, with five candidates per query, and four of the ten engines come from one vendor. Decision models were run with one state and one set of questions, written once and not tuned. Engines change, and the labels describe answers collected in 2026.

8 Reproducibility

Release.

GEO Citation Ranker 4B is released at https://huggingface.co/citead/geo-citation-ranker-4b, with the adapters of the two other 4B seeds and of the 0.6B student, under the Apache 2.0 license of its base model. The benchmark is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/citead/geo-citation-benchmark. It contains the 1145 evaluation passages, the 6345 citation labels with engine and query, the fold assignment, the predictions of the 36 scorer configurations of this paper on every evaluation passage, the 757 training groups without labels, and the code. Passages and labels are released under CC BY-SA 4.0, the license of GEO-Bench.

Regimes.

The tables and the figure are regenerated offline from the released benchmark, at no API cost. code/reproduce_tables.py recomputes the correlations and paired differences, code/analyses.py the cross-engine agreement, baselines, top-1 accuracy, per-engine and per-query means and the overlap check, and paper/make_tables.py and paper/make_figures.py write the tables and the figure. The agreement between the two teachers is computed on labels that are not released. To retrain a student, code/label_jev.py labels the training groups with Jev for about 0.10 USD and code/train_student.py trains on those labels.

Not released.

The teacher labels are not released. The LLM-judge rubric is given in Appendix B.

Disclosures.

The authors are employed by TW3 Partners, which offers generative engine visibility services under the Citead name.

9 Conclusion

On ten engines under controlled retrieval, the strongest predictors of which source an answer engine cites are decision models that compare the candidates together, hosted or open. GEO Citation Ranker 4B, a 4B reranker distilled from teacher labels, is not distinguishable from them on 229 queries, and the labels it needs cost a few cents. The engines agree with one another well above every scorer we measured, so the benchmark leaves room for scorers that compare candidates jointly. Any new scorer can be placed against the same groups, the engines’ own agreement and the same intervals.

Appendix A Engines

The 4B student ranges from 0.446 on llama-3.3-70b-instruct to 0.607 on gemma-4-31b-it, Jev from 0.461 to 0.650, and the student stays above the NIM reranker on every engine. gpt-oss-120b gives a zero share to 67% of sources, which leaves 44 non-degenerate groups out of 80 queries. Averaged with equal weight per engine, the 4B student scores 0.534, Jev 0.572 and JEV-27B 0.576.

Appendix B Prompts and rubrics

Decision models.

The state lists the query and the passages, each truncated to 250 words. The question for passage kk reads: “Considering the QUERY and comparing PASSAGE kk against the four other passages, rate the share of citation PASSAGE kk would receive if a generative answer engine wrote an answer to the query drawing on these 5 sources. Judge RELATIVE to the other passages. Direct relevance to the query dominates; then citable facts, statistics, quotability, apparent authority, and self-containment. Do not reward length by itself.” The six levels are 0, not cited at all; 1, marginal; 2, minor source; 3, moderate source; 4, major source; and 5, dominant source, each with a one-line description in the code. The pointwise protocol asks the same question about a single passage.

LLM judge.

The judge receives a query and five passages in a seeded random order, truncated to 250 words, and returns a score from 0 to 100 per passage for the expected citation share relative to the other four. The rubric ranks, in order, direct relevance to the query, density of citable information, figures and dates, quotability, apparent authority and self-containment. It instructs the judge not to reward length, to give less to a passage redundant with a better one, and to ignore presentation order.

Students.

The input is “Given a user query, judge whether this passage would be cited by a generative answer engine (Perplexity, ChatGPT Search, Gemini) writing an answer to the query”, followed by the query and the passage, in the Qwen3-Reranker template. The score is the log-odds of the “yes” token against the “no” token.
